| [LIT-047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-047.md) v2 | Is It Good to Cooperate? Testing the Theory of Morality-as-Cooperation in 60 Societies | Curry et al. (2019), DOI-10.1086/701478. In the ethnographic records of the 60-society HRAF Probability Sample, seven cooperative behaviours predicted by game theory are morally valenced positively in 961 of 962 observations (99.9%). | [LIT-120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-120.md) v2 | Welfare Subjects and Autopoiesis | Bruckner (2025), DOI-10.1017/apa.2025.10006. Bruckner proposes, by abduction and not deduction (§4), that being autopoietic is sufficient, not necessary, for being a welfare subject. | [LIT-125](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-125.md) v2 | The moral psychology of obligation | Tomasello (2019), DOI-10.1017/S0140525X19001742. Tomasello proposes that the human sense of obligation is "the internalized social/rational pressure from a joint or collective self-regulating agent 'we'… to do what 'we' expect me to" (§3). It arises first, around age 3, inside joint-commitment collaboration with a partner, and then, from about 3–5 years, toward in-group members through collective identification. The support is a synthesis of developmental and comparative experiments, mostly from his own lab, on WEIRD children versus chimpanzees; the paper runs no new experiment. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md)); worth reading as the standard statement of the shared-intentionality account of obligation and, above all, as a treatment. | [LIT-138](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-138.md) v2 | The Depth of the Body | Register (2025), DOI-10.3998/phimp.7576. Register argues that body parthood "for moral purposes" is bounded below by depth. Depth is the microphysical commitment of an object's real definition, and objects that are "too deep" (a water molecule, the parcel of matter now composing the heart, a particular cloud server) are not body parts, though they are parts in the ordinary sense. His two principles ("bodily interests/rights are high-level") say that events which are high-level neutral do not bear on bodily rights or interests. So a BCI user's implemented software can be a body part owned by the user while the third-party server that runs it is not. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-151.md)); worth reading as a short, clearly argued proposal that separates a moral "body-part" relation from ordinary parthood by level of abstraction, and applies it to cloud-hosted BCIs. | [LIT-146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-146.md) v2 | The Moral Status of Animals | Gruen & Monsó (2003), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/moral-animal/>. The entry reviews five proposed grounds of moral considerability (species membership, human-exceptional capacities, personhood, sentience and agency). Its conclusion is that attempts to establish human uniqueness by capacities are "not the most promising" (§1.2). It then separates *having* moral status from the *weight* of a claim ("showing up on a moral radar screen", §2.2). Weight depends on the value theory adopted for animal interests (hedonism, preference satisfaction, objective list; §2.1) and on the normative framework (rights, which are absolute but generate forward-looking duties when violated, or a multi-factor utilitarianism). It closes with virtue-ethical, feminist, relational and empathy-based approaches that reject argument from capacities altogether (§3). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md)); worth reading as the standard current survey of the grounds and weighing of animals' moral status. It is balanced for most of its length, but §2.2 argues at length for a multi-factor utilitarian view and §3 ends on Gruen's own "entangled empathy", so cite it for the map, not as neutral on the weighing. |

| [LIT-182](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-182.md) v3 | Towards ethical evolution: responsible autonomy of artificial intelligence across generations | Terziyan et al. (2025), DOI-10.1007/s43681-025-00759-9. The paper proposes, without implementation, formalism or experiment, that an AI system which designs further AI systems should pass on one "immutable" principle. The principle is: do not directly harm humanity or violate fundamental human values; monitor and mitigate misuse of your outputs; and make every derivative inherit this principle (p. 12). The mechanisms are a genetic-algorithm analogy, with immutable and mutable "genes", constrained crossover and filtered mutation, together with "temporal cloning". The paper is inconsistent about its central notion. The principle is enforced once by a penalty F = Q − α·P (p. 9) and once by "unbreachable" hard constraints (p. 13). And it is "immutable" only in its architecture, while its ethical content stays "adaptable" (p. 14). | Rejected — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-156](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-156.md)); not worth a reader's time. It is a programme statement whose one concrete proposal is contradicted by the paper's own later sections. It demonstrates nothing, even though its conclusion says it does (p. 21). It does not engage the alignment work on preserving goals across successors that the problem calls for. A reader interested in value preservation under recursive self-design would do better starting from that literature. |
